titre: A charred beam closed a four-century gap
accroche: In 1929, a beam found in Arizona links two tree-ring chronologies that had remained separate, and finally gives the ruins of the American Southwest a calendar
contenu_vulgarise:
In the 1900s, the astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass, at Lowell Observatory in Arizona, was looking for a link between solar activity and Earth's climate. His idea: tree growth rings, wider in rainy years and narrower in dry ones, should record the cycles of the sun. To test it, he needed a ring chronology reaching back as far in time as possible.

Douglass built two separate series. The first, from living trees and the timbers of recent buildings, goes back step by step to around 1400. The second, from charred beams taken from prehistoric ruins of the American Southwest, forms a continuous sequence of 586 years, but a floating one: it shows the relative order of the rings, without anyone knowing which calendar year it corresponds to.

## The gap, then the beam that closes it

Between the two series lay an interval of unknown length. No beam found so far had rings old enough to reach the modern chronology and recent enough to reach the floating one.

On June 22, 1929, during a third expedition funded by the National Geographic Society, Douglass's team extracted a charred beam from the site of Show Low, Arizona. Its code name was HH-39. Its most recent rings overlap the oldest end of the modern chronology by forty-nine years. All at once the two series joined into a single continuous scale, reaching back to around the year 700.

Every ruin already excavated in the region could now be given an exact date, and not just a relative place in a pottery sequence. Pueblo Bonito, in Chaco Canyon, is dated to the late 11th century. Aztec Ruin, farther north, to the years 1110 to 1121. Douglass published these results as early as December 1929, then in 1937 founded the Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research at the University of Arizona, still one of the discipline's leading centers.

## The detour

Dendrochronology was not born of an archaeological question. Douglass was looking for sunspots in wood, not construction dates. In trying to extend his own chronology, for his own purposes, he gave Southwestern archaeology, as a by-product, something it had never had: an absolute calendar, year by year, independent of any assumption about pottery style or the rate at which layers accumulate.

The method has since gone beyond its original territory. Tree-ring sequences far longer than Douglass's are now used to calibrate radiocarbon dating itself, whose raw results must be corrected year by year.

repere.texte: On June 22, 1929, at Show Low (Arizona), beam HH-39 closes the gap between Douglass's two chronologies: its most recent rings overlap the oldest end of the modern chronology by forty-nine years, tying the ruins of the American Southwest to a precise calendar year for the first time.
repere.source: Douglass, “The Secret of the Southwest Solved by Talkative Tree Rings,” The National Geographic Magazine, 56 (6), December 1929, pp. 736-770

carte.punch: A charred beam linked two chronologies separated by centuries
carte.idee: The astronomer Andrew Douglass had built two ring sequences with no link between them, a modern one and a prehistoric floating one. On June 22, 1929, a beam found at Show Low, Arizona, closes the gap and gives the ruins of the American Southwest an absolute calendar, back to around the year 700.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English. The full career, from astronomy to the founding of dendrochronology.

quiz.question: Why did beam HH-39 make it possible to date Pueblo Bonito and other ruins precisely?
choix: Because its rings link up with both the floating chronology and the modern one
Because it was found directly beneath the foundations of Pueblo Bonito
Because its exceptional size made it the oldest known beam at the site
Because it bore an engraved inscription mentioning a construction date
quiz.explication: The bridge between the two chronologies rests on the forty-nine-year overlap of the rings, not on where it was found, the beam's size, or an inscription: no beam of that period bears a written date, and it is the ring count that makes the calendar.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Douglass looking for when he built his ring chronologies?
choix: A construction date for the ruins of the American Southwest
A link between solar activity and Earth's climate
A method for correcting radiocarbon dating results
The origin of the wood species used in ancient timbers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Douglass was an astronomer at Lowell Observatory: he was looking for the trace of the sun's cycles in the width of the rings, wider in rainy years. The calendar he gave archaeology came as a by-product.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is a floating chronology, like Douglass's prehistoric series?
choix: A series whose rings are not spaced one year apart
A series reconstructed from submerged wood, and therefore poorly preserved
A series that gives the order of the rings with no corresponding calendar year
A series whose exact length remains unknown for lack of samples
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The prehistoric sequence of 586 years was continuous, but nothing said which calendar years it corresponded to: it showed the relative order of the rings, and nothing more. The forty-nine-year overlap provided by HH-39 anchored it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are even longer ring sequences used for today?
choix: To calibrate radiocarbon dating, whose results must be corrected
To replace radiocarbon dating, judged too imprecise
To date pottery whose style can no longer establish its place in a sequence
To reconstruct the position of sunspots century by century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The method has gone beyond its original territory: sequences far longer than Douglass's are used to correct, year by year, the raw results of radiocarbon dating.
